author: Dividend Sleuth
title: Screening Closed End Funds
text:
A June 3, 2018 article, " BDCs: I Put Up The Rake ," reviewed my history with business development companies. Today’s article reviews my experience with closed end funds. I did better with CEFs than BDCs, but the CEF experience was unsatisfying because I was becoming a short-term trader rather than a long-term investor.
Even worse, I cannot explain my rationale for buying and selling the CEFs. I bought when I saw a recommendation by Douglas Albo or Left Banker, for example, and I sold when there was a nice profit. In some cases, when a CEF dropped and then neared my cost basis, I would sell it. I operated from greed and fear rather than a clear buy/sell philosophy. I was successful because I had access to some keen minds.
Here’s a brief summary of my CEF experience, divided into two periods:
In 28 months from October 31, 2011 through March 3, 2014, I bought and sold 9 CEFs. The average holding period was 6.7 months. The average annualized gain was 17.57%, excluding distributions. In 19 months from May 3, 2016 through December 1, 2017, I bought and sold 10 CEFs. The average holding period was 6.1 months. The average annualized gain was 8.11%, excluding distributions. Sometimes I made one purchase and one sale, but in most cases there were multiple purchases and in some cases multiple sales:

I want to maintain an awareness of BDCs, CEFs and energy MLPs by making a small investment in each category.
In preparation for a possible new entry into the world of BDCs and CEFs, I took a step back to develop a strategy for how to approach these entities. Here's my approach to closed end funds.
A "Nominating Committee" There are many moving parts with CEFs. I want to tap the best and most experienced minds available on Seeking Alpha. CEFs seem to move randomly with swings in "investor sentiment." From time to time Doug Albo points out irrationality in the CEF market .
I consider some of the Seeking Alpha CEF practitioners as a "Nominating Committee" to provide a starting point for studying CEFs: Douglas Albo, Left Banker, Stanford Chemist and Nick Ackerman. William Stamm writes mostly about individual equities, but he has written about several Eaton Vance closed end funds. From Steven Bavaria's list of high yield investments, and you can glean several CEF ideas.
Just over a year ago (in June, 2017), Bob Wells wrote two blog entries ( here and here ) about his desire to learn more about closed end funds. In his typical style, Bob engaged the Seeking Alpha community to help him develop a strategy. If you’re a newcomer to CEFs, the comments following Bob’s two blog entries would be a fruitful place to begin a study of CEFs.
Gleaning some CEF ideas Douglas Albo’s June 25, 2018 article nominated several CEFs, including the AllianzGI NFJ Dividend Interest & Premium Strategy Fund (NYSE: NFJ ):
"The AllianzGI Equity & Convertible Income Fund (NYSE: NIE ), $22.40 market price, 24.04 NAV, -6.8% discount, 6.8% current market yield, has been a great performer over the last few years and there was a time when its much larger cousin, the $1.37 billion NFJ Dividend & Premium Strategy Fund ( NFJ ), $12.89 market price, $14.46 NAV, -10.9% discount, 7.0% current market yield, traded at a much narrower discount than NIE despite NIE's more growth oriented portfolio and minimal use of option writing.
"But as NIE's superior NAV performance allowed the fund to raise its distribution (something I wrote about several times while endorsing NIE over NFJ), NFJ was forced to cut not once but twice over the last few years and it's been NFJ that has fallen out of favor and now trades at a -10.9% discount.
"But if you believe that for the markets to advance from here, value stocks will need some kind of rotation, then it might make sense finally to swap out of NIE and into NFJ."
Left Banker’s June 11, 2018 article (paywalled) nominated the Liberty All­-Stars Growth Fund (NYSE: ASG ):
"First thing to note is that ASG is an unleveraged fund that does not use option strategies to generate income. This sets it outside the standard run of equity CEFs where one or the other of those strategies, sometimes both, prevail. ...
"Distribution yield for ASG is 7.27%, which is a solid payout for an unleveraged domestic-equity fund. The distribution is paid quarterly. The fund does not have a managed distribution, so the quarterly distribution varies with the fund’s fortunes. ...
"For 2017, the distribution sources were ordinary dividends (6.8% qualified, 17.3% non-qualified) and long-term capital gains (75.9%). For 2014 through 2016 distributions were 100% sourced from long-term capital gains. Thus, the distribution is reasonably tax efficient. ...
"What I like about ASG is the fund’s consistently solid performance record, its distribution policy, and its reasonable valuation. ...
"Finally, as I’ve noted, the top-performing CEFs are strongly overvalued at this time. Typically, CEF investors look for discounts. The top performers from the list of fifteen have an average premium of 5.0%. By that measure, ASG’s near-par valuation is attractive."
Stanford Chemist’s year-ago July 6, 2017 article (paywalled) about the BlackRock Enhanced Capital and Income Fund (NYSE: CII ) brought this CEF into my consciousness. The Chemist compared CII with the Nuveen S&P 500 Dynamic Overwrite Fund ( SPXX ). Please note this article is a year old :
"There are some minor differences between the strategy of CII and SPXX. CII writes single stock covered calls, with 46% of the portfolio having been overwritten as of the latest annual report. In contrast, SPXX has a 'dynamic' call writing strategy that targets 55% coverage, but that can vary between 35 to 75% depending on the market environment. Additionally, SPXX can write index options, single stock options, and basket options.
"In terms of portfolio, SPXX matches closely with the S&P 500, while CII has a significant active component, although it is still largely focused on U.S. large cap stocks. Both funds have Apple ( AAPL ), Google ( GOOG ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) as their top 3 holdings, with CII running the more concentrated portfolio of the two. CII's 5th to 10th place holdings (Comcast ( CMCSA ), Bank of America ( BAC ), Carnival Corp. ( CCL ), Dow Chemical (DOW), Pfizer ( PFE ), and Home Depot ( HD )), while not among the S&P 500's top 10 largest constituents, are still very recognizable large cap names.
"Performance-wise, it is actually CII that has been the better fund in NAV terms over the past 1, 3, 5 and 10-year periods. (Note that return periods longer than 1 year are annualized)."
William Stamm’s April 16, 2018 article (paywalled) about Eaton Vance Tax­Managed Buy-Write­ Opportunities Fund (NYSE: ETV ) reminded me of this former holding and put it on the table for consideration:
"Being in retirement, my goal is to have a steady monthly income, without the swings of dividends that are paid on a quarterly or yearly basis. The ETV fund distribution of 8.9%/year (0.1108$/Month) return in today's low interest rate environment is fantastic and gives my income companies a solid footing.
"I calculated the total return of ETV over a 51 month test period starting with January 1, 2014 till April 2018 YTD, 51 months in total. I chose this time because it includes the great year of 2017, and other years that had fair and bad performance. ETV outperformed the DOW average by 1.17%. For the 51 month test period, the DOW total return was 48.18% and ETV beat it at 49.35%. ETV does really well in an up market and is following the market in this volatile up market YTD. The economy seems to be moving forward which is good for ETV with its covered call approach to dampen the swings of the market."
Steven Bavaria’s February 26, 2018 blog post indirectly nominated the Cohen & Steers Total Return Realty Fund (NYSE: RFI ) . Steven’s blog post included a reference to the Cohen & Steers Closed-End Opportunity Fund (NYSE: FOF ), which caused me to check out a former holding ( RFI ). It trades at a slight discount to NAV. It has a 10-year NAV growth rate of over 9% and it has the lowest fees of the five I've highlighted from the screen.
Nick Ackerman’s June 21, 2018 article nominated the BlackRock Health Sciences Trust (NYSE: BME ) . This caught my attention:
"The 10-year annualized returns can be compared with the broader market when looking at the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) 10-year returns of 9.75%. When looking back at that period, BME is crushing the market by far on a NAV and market price basis.
"The monthly distribution is even attractive at a 6.28% distribution rate, paid on a monthly schedule."
I read several positive comments by readers about the Eaton Vance Enhanced Equity Income Fund II (NYSE: EOS ) . Nick, William and Doug have written about EOS. After some reading, I added this CEF to the short list of CEFs to study. However, EOS has appreciated dramatically in 2018 and trades at premium. This may not be a good time to buy, but EOS may be a good CEF to put on a watchlist. Here are excerpts from Nick Ackerman's May 26, 2018 (paywalled) article:
"EOS has total net assets of $756.8 million as of their last Fact Sheet available on March 31, 2018. The fund has a primary investment objective to provide current income, and a secondary objective of capital appreciation. The fund attempts to achieve this by investing primarily in large and mid-cap securities that the investment advisor believes have above-average growth and financial strength and also writes call options on individual securities to generate income from option premium. The latest fact sheet shows that 48% of the stock portfolio have call options written. The fund offers a managed distribution plan. ...
"The fund has returned almost 20% YTD. While this is impressive, the NAV return has not kept up. The NAV YTD sits at a return of 8.48%, which is still impressive in itself. With such a drastic rise for 2018, the fund has increased its premium to 6.36% over NAV. The current share price is at $17.72, with a NAV price of $16.66. The 1-year average is actually a 1.62% discount. This gives EOS a z-score of 3.90. This would indicate that EOS is richly valued compared to its history, and when looking at the premium/discount chart since inception, it would appear this is very unusual.
"...EOS does not generally trade at a premium, or when it does, it does not tend to hold the premium for very long."
A screen for studying CEFs I offer this simple screening process to you as an example of how one person is approaching CEFs. Our preferences and our risk tolerance will vary. If you have a screening process in place, I encourage you to share it with us. Also, I welcome your suggestions about how to improve my screening process.
I’ve created a spreadsheet (excerpts from which are duplicated below) for my CEF watchlist. This spreadsheet contains the items I want to monitor to help me decide which CEF(s) to purchase and at what price.

Leverage
My first screen greatly reduces the universe of CEFs for consideration. I've chosen not to invest in CEFs that use leverage in a significant way.
Net Asset Value growth over time
I'm looking for CEFs that have grown their net asset value, or NAV, over time. For almost a decade, we have enjoyed one of the great bull markets of history. Surely, I reasoned, an effective management team could grow a fund’s net asset value by at least 1.0% annually for the past decade.
There’s an easy tool for this that is readily available from Morningstar . The "Quote" tab is the start-up page when you pull up Morningstar data for a CEF. Scroll down the left side of the page. Just after "Valuation Statistics," you will see "Total Returns" for the CEF. You can pull up the annual NAV growth rate several time periods: 1 day, 1 month, 3 months, 1 year, 3 years, 5 years and 10 years. I click on the "10Y" option and it shows me the annual growth rate as a numerical percentage and as a bar graph. I want good management, and a growing NAV is one way to evaluate how well management has performed over time. The 10 year growth rates are shown in the table above.
Fees
I want a CEF with low fees. I arbitrarily determined a 1.25% maximum for annual fees. I have a column on my spreadsheet for fees (as reported by Morningstar and by the CEFs).
Writing options
I'm comfortable with CEFs that writes call options as a way of gaining extra income for the fund. So, I note on my spreadsheet whether or not a CEF uses option writing as a tool.
Assessing risk
Morningstar rates CEFs using a "star" system, with 5 stars being the highest and 1 star being the lowest. Here’s what Investopedia says about the Morningstar rating system:
"The Morningstar risk rating is a ranking given to publicly traded (funds) by the investment research firm Morningstar. … Morningstar's risk ratings, also called star ratings, are designed to help investors quickly identify funds to consider for their portfolios.
"Debuted in 1985, Morningstar risk ratings are based on the fund's past performance, the fund manager's skill, risk- and cost-adjusted returns, and performance consistency. Morningstar assigns a one-star rating to 10% of the funds it evaluates, a two-star rating to 22.5% of funds, a three-star rating to 35% of funds, a four-star rating to 22.5% of funds. and a five-star rating to 10% of funds. The Morningstar ratings are intended to be a starting point for further research and are not buy or sell recommendations.
"Using objective mathematical tools, Morningstar evaluates funds for up to three time periods: three, five and 10 years. It combines the ratings for each of these time periods to create an overall rating for the fund. The agency does not evaluate funds with less than three years of history.”
Consulting other analysts
Beyond Seeking Alpha, my first stop usually is Morningstar. Their excellent free information provides ample data to determine whether a CEF merits further research. Nuveen's CEFConnect website provides helpful information and a tool to screen CEFs. I read material provided by each CEF and I perform an Internet search by entering the name of the CEF being studied.
A summary of criteria for Quality and Performance
If I'm serious enough about a CEF to consult a variety of analyst/contributor opinions, the CEF is in the "serious consideration" category. Here's a summary of the checklist:
No leverage; Writes options to generate income; Good management reflected in a history of NAV growth; Reasonable fees; and Four or five stars from Morningstar. I see fees as reasonable and I am comfortable with what some respected voices have said about the CEF. At this point, I'm ready to try to determine an appropriate price for establishing a position. The screening process continues as I develop a target buy price by considering several factors.
Screening for Valuation Once I've determined that a CEF would be a welcomed addition to my retirement income portfolio, it's time to consider whether it currently trades at an attractive price.
Context for current valuation
One of my weaknesses in the past was my willingness to jump into a position without studying the current price and net asset value in relation to the CEF's history. This time, I am determined to gain some working knowledge (and hopefully insight) about a fund's history of net asset value and market price. I keep two columns on my spreadsheet for the 52-week high and low price. Morningstar provides the NAV and price history for recent years. In the past, I wasn’t patient to look for where the CEF was in relation to its historic price swings—both short term (52-weeks) and long term (last 5 years)—and in relation to the relationship between market price and NAV.
Relationship with 52-week high price
A column on my spreadsheet calculates the percentage difference between the current price and the CEF's 52-week high price. If the current price is considerably lower, I want to know if there is something internal to the CEF or something about the broader economy/market that has driven it lower. Is this a warning sign or an indicator of a buying opportunity (or both)?
Relationship with recent low prices
How does the present price compare with the 52-week low price? If it is considerably higher, what has driven up the CEF’s market price? Usually, this is a sign for me to slow down and wait for a pullback in price. I also look for the low price over the past 3 to 5 years. I use Seeking Alpha’s simple orange price graph that accompanies each holding. I like to look at several of the time frame alternatives available. The "default" graph is 1 year. This gives me a visualization of the 52-week price range. I also take a look at the 6 month graph and the 1 month graph, just to get an idea of any recent price movements or trends. The 5 year graph and the 10 year graph are helpful for seeing how the fund has performed over the longer term. These multiple time frames give me some background for determining a desirable entry point.
(10 year graph for BME from Seeking Alpha )
Does the present price reflect a discount to net asset value?
Obviously, all things being equal, I prefer a discount to a premium. However, I'm more interested in where the present premium/discount is relative to the CEF’s past rather than a comparison with other CEFs. This is similar to a stock’s price/earnings ratio. When I compare a stock’s P/E ratio with that of another company—particularly if it's in another sector—the comparison is less helpful than a comparison of the stock’s present P/E to its own historic P/E trends. Some stocks consistently receive what Chuck Carnevale calls a "premium valuation" from the market. This can be true for CEFs, though my observation is that the price swings in premium/discount to NAV are more frequent and more dramatic with CEFs. In my previous attempts to invest in CEFs, I didn’t take a long enough historic view to appreciate these swings. I was too focused on the current price and sometimes learned that I should have waited to find a more attractive entry point.
I use my spreadsheet to document the present price/NAV relationship compared to the historic price/NAV relationship. One column on the spreadsheet indicates the current discount or premium. Morningstar provides the high, low and average discount for each of the previous 5 years (plus year-to-date information). From the Morningstar data I note the 5-year high discount and the 5-year low discount, and I calculate the 5 calculate the average discount. I like to do this myself because the mental exercise helps me internalize the CEF’s history. Morningstar’s "Quote" page provides the 3 year average premium or discount and the 6 month average premium or discount. This serves a check to make sure I calculated the data correctly.
If I like the CEF and its current discount to NAV is close to its 3 or 5 year average discount, I begin to look for reasons not to buy it at the current price.
The Z-statistic
Left Banker’s June 11 article explains the z-statistic:
"Briefly, Z-scores for CEFs tell us how far the current premium/discount valuation is from the funds mean valuation. A negative Z-score means the fund is more discounted than the mean. The value of the Z-score is the number of standard deviations from the mean the current valuation is."
So, I'm looking (and perhaps waiting) for a negative Z-score.
Statistics How To provides an explanation of the Z-statistic in mathematics.
Yield
In determining a target buy price for a CEF, my final screen is the current yield. I compare a CEF's current yield with its historic yield and how it compares with other CEFs. My question is not whether this CEF provides the highest possible yield. Rather, it's whether the present yield is attractive relative to this CEF’s historic yield. Even this is not absolute, because yield trends are impacted by many "macro" factors, including Federal Reserve policy and the broader economic environment. When I read SA articles and comments about CEFs, sometimes I get the impression that the only relevant metric is whether CEF "A" has a higher yield than CEF "B." For me, the current yield is not the first screen, but rather the last screen. I want to be informed by a CEF's yield but not seduced by it.
A summary of criteria for Valuation
Here's a brief checklist of what I look for in valuation:
How does the present NAV and price compare with the CEF's recent and long term history? Specifically, does a recent low price (last year or two) represent a possible target entry point? Is the present price a discount to NAV? How does the present discount compare with the CEF's historic discount (see Morningstar). Is the present yield attractive relative to the CEF's history? Does the yield fairly compensate for the known potential risks? Conclusion Based on this screening process, my current top choice is the BlackRock Health Sciences Trust ( BME ). However, I'm not persuaded to buy any of the CEFs at today's prices. BME is the only CEF in the process that has managed to grow its net asset value by at least 1% a year over the past decade. If you know of another CEF that has grown NAV in this range or better, please let me know.
I eliminated NFJ and ASG from immediate consideration because I need to do more study. NFJ has a low Morningstar risk rating and a low 10-year NAV growth rate. ASG trades at a 13% premium to NAV.
Of the 5 remaining CEFs on my watchlist, BME is the one I'm watching most closely.
I welcome your opinion about CEFs and I'm eager to learn how you screen the CEF universe for investment ideas. Your comments enrich our discussion. I always learn from our Seeking Alpha conversations.
It's not my intent to advocate the purchase or sale of any security. My purpose is to offer ideas for stocks to study and to share a journal of my effort to design and build a retirement portfolio that puts a priority on relative safety, a history of dividend growth and solid future prospects. Your goals and risk tolerance may differ, so please do your own due diligence.
